newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Megawati lauds human rights commission.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Megawati lauds human rights commission.

text.p: Megawati Sukarnoputri, ousted leader of the opposition Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), said on Saturday a report by Indonesia's official human rights body on riots in Jakarta on July 27 was "independent and brave".

She said in a statement that she respected the Indonesian Commission on Human Rights for its report on the riots, which erupted after police raided the PDI headquarters in Jakarta to evict her supporters from the building.
It was the worst violence in the city for more than two decades and left at least five people dead and scores of buildings and vehicles gutted by fire.
"The PDI respects the (commission) for its objectivity...and for putting the nation above individual groups," Megawati said.
She said that the commission had been "independent and brave" in its report and in the defence of human rights.

Megawati, daughter of late founding president Sukarno, was ousted as leader of the PDI in June this year after a government-backed congress elected deputy parliamentary speaker Surjadi as leader in her place.

Megawati has not accepted the decision, saying she had been lawfully elected as PDI leader for a five-year term in 1993. Her supporters refused to vacate the party headquarters in central Jakarta after the congress.
The riots erupted after police and around 200 supporters of Surjadi raided the headquarters to evict Megawati's supporters from the building.

The commission, which was set up by presidential decree in 1993, said in a report on the riots that the government had involved itself "excessively and in a biased way" in the internal problems of the PDI.
The report called on the government to take legal action against Surjadi supporters who attacked the headquarters.
The trials of 124 people arrested in or around the party headquarters began earlier this month but lawyers say all are members or supporters of Megawati's faction of the PDI.
In the statement, Megawati said that the she agreed with these recommendations and called for the rule of law in Indonesia.
Political analysts have said that the government moved to sideline Megawati because it feared she could draw votes away from Indonesia's ruling Golkar party in next year's parliamentary elections.
Golkar, ending its annual congress on Friday, said that it hopes to increase its vote in 1997 to 71 percent after obtaining 68 percent in 1992.
The Christian-Nationalist PDI, the ruling Golkar and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) are the only groups legally allowed to contest elections.
